The verb "to index" means to create or establish a connection between something and a reference point, so that the thing can be found, tracked, or adjusted using that reference. Think of an index as a bridge — "to index" means to build that bridge.

The word has four distinct but closely related meanings depending on the context. Once you understand them all, you'll see they all share this same soul.
Meaning 1: To Organize Information So It Can Be Found

This is the oldest and most literal meaning.

When you index something, you go through it carefully, identify its important parts, and record where each part can be found — so that anyone looking for something specific can locate it instantly without reading everything.

You've seen the result of this at the back of a textbook: a list of topics with page numbers next to them. Someone had to create that list. The act of creating it is called indexing the book.

Example: "The editor spent three days indexing the 600-page manual."

This means the editor read through the entire manual, pulled out every important term and topic, noted which pages they appeared on, and arranged them in alphabetical order. Now a reader can look up "safety procedures" and immediately know to go to page 312.

A person whose job is to do this professionally is called an indexer. It takes real skill — you must decide what is important enough to include, how to word it, and how to organize it so readers can find what they need intuitively.

The same logic applies digitally. When Google "indexes" a web page, it visits the page, reads and analyzes all its content, and stores organized information about it in its massive system. Later, when you search for something, Google doesn't read the whole internet live — it looks through its index, finds which pages are relevant, and shows them to you in seconds. To index here means to bring something into a searchable, organized reference system.
Meaning 2: To Link One Thing to Another So They Move Together

This is the economic and financial meaning, and it's extremely important.

When you index one value to another, you are tying them together so that when one changes, the other automatically changes by the same proportion.

Example: "The government indexed pensions to inflation."

This means: pensions are now permanently tied to inflation. If inflation rises by 4%, pensions automatically rise by 4%. They move together, in lockstep. Nobody has to make a separate decision each year — the connection is built in.

This is done to protect people (or values) from being left behind. If your salary stays the same but prices keep rising, you are getting poorer in real terms. Indexing your salary to inflation means your salary grows automatically to keep up — your purchasing power stays stable.

Here are more examples of this meaning:

  • "Her rent is indexed to the consumer price index." → Her rent rises automatically each year in line with the official measure of how much prices have gone up.
  • "The tax brackets are indexed to wages." → As average wages rise, the income levels at which tax rates kick in also rise, so workers aren't pushed into higher tax brackets simply because of inflation.
  • "The loan repayments were indexed to the bank's base interest rate." → When the interest rate goes up, the repayments go up. When the rate falls, the repayments fall.

The key idea is automatic, proportional adjustment. You're not just saying "these two things are related." You're building in a mechanism so they move together without anyone having to intervene each time.
Meaning 3: To Record and Categorize Within a Database or System

This is closely related to Meaning 1, but it lives more in the world of computing and information management.

When a system (or a person) indexes a piece of data, it means they bring that item into a structured catalog and assign it the right labels, codes, or positions so it can be searched and retrieved efficiently later.

Example: "The library indexes every new article by subject, author, and publication year."

This means each article is processed and entered into the system with tags attached to it. Later, a researcher can search "climate change + 2024" and the system immediately surfaces all relevant articles — because they were indexed with those terms.

In computer science, indexing a database table means creating a special data structure that allows searches to run much faster. Instead of the computer checking every single row to find what you're looking for, it can consult the index and jump straight to the right location. To index is to create that shortcut.
Meaning 4: To Point To or Indicate Something (Academic/Linguistic Use)

This meaning appears mostly in academic writing, linguistics, and philosophy — less in everyday conversation, but worth knowing.

In this sense, to index something means to serve as a sign that points to it or signals its presence.

Examples:

  • "A high fever indexes serious illness." → A high fever is a signal, a pointer, an indicator that something serious is happening in the body.
  • "His nervous laugh indexed his anxiety." → His laugh was pointing to — giving away — the anxiety underneath.
  • "Smoke indexes fire." → Smoke doesn't just remind us of fire; it is a direct indicator that fire is present or was present.

The difference between indicating and indexing here is subtle but precise. In technical language, when we say something indexes something else, we mean the connection is direct and natural — not symbolic, not arbitrary. Smoke doesn't symbolize fire. It directly points to it because it is physically caused by it. That's what makes it an index rather than just a symbol.

You don't need to memorize this distinction for everyday use, but if you encounter "indexes" in an academic text, this is likely what it means.

Here's how to remember all four meanings as one idea:

To index always means to establish a structured, reliable connection between something and a reference point — whether that reference is a page number, a price level, a database category, or a cause. The purpose is always the same: to make something trackable, findable, or tied to something else in a principled way.

In Meaning 1, you connect a topic to its location in a book or system.
In Meaning 2, you connect a value to a measure so they move in tandem.
In Meaning 3, you connect a piece of data to a searchable catalog.

How It's Used in Real Life

You'll most often encounter this word in these situations:

In everyday language, you'll hear "indexed to inflation" or "indexed to the cost of living" in news about salaries, pensions, taxes, and government benefits. This is Meaning 2, and it's very common.

In technology news, you'll hear "Google indexed the page" or "this content hasn't been indexed yet," meaning Meaning 3 — the content has or hasn't been brought into a searchable system.

In publishing and academia, "to index a book" or "the article is indexed in this database" refers to Meaning 1 and 3.

In philosophy, semiotics, or linguistics papers, "indexes" or "indexing" in Meaning 4 will appear when a scholar discusses signs and what they point to.
One Sentence to Tie It All Together
To index means to create a structured, reliable connection between something and a reference point — so that it can be located, tracked, adjusted, or understood in relation to something else.
